## 1. Read in the data

```{r}
met <- read.csv("~/Downloads/met_all.gz")
```

The meteorological dataset contains weather-station readings collected from stations in the continental United States.

## 2. Check the dimensions, headers, and footers

```{r}
dim(met)
head(met)
tail(met)
```

The dataset has r nrow(met) rows and r ncol(met) columns.

## 3. Examine the variables

```{r}
str(met)
```

This output shows the names, data types, and example values of the variables in the dataset.

## 4. Examine the key variables

```{r}
table(met$year)
table(met$day)
table(met$hour)

summary(met$temp)
summary(met$elev)
summary(met$wind.sp)
```

The elevation variable contains values of 9999.0. Based on the data documentation and the implausibility of this elevation for a weather station in the continental United States, these values appear to represent missing observations. Therefore, they are replaced with `NA`.


```{r}
met$elev[met$elev == 9999.0] <- NA
summary(met$elev)
```

### Highest weather-station elevation


```{r}
max_elevation <- max(met$elev, na.rm = TRUE)
max_elevation
```

The highest valid weather-station elevation in the dataset is r max_elevation meters.

### Examine unusually low temperatures

```{r}
met <- met[is.na(met$temp) | met$temp > -40, ]

met2 <- met[order(met$temp), ]
head(met2)
```

After removing temperatures of −40°C or colder, an observation with a temperature of approximately −17.2°C remains and requires further investigation.

## 5. Check suspicious values

The suspicious temperature observation can be examined using its geographic coordinates and station information.


```{r}
met[!is.na(met$temp) & met$temp <= -15, ]
```

The unusually low observations were checked against the location and expected climate of the weather station. Because the values were inconsistent with the location and the rest of the dataset, temperatures of −15°C or colder were removed.


```{r}
met <- met[is.na(met$temp) | met$temp > -15, ]

met2 <- met[order(met$temp), ]
head(met2)

summary(met$temp)
```

After removing temperatures of −15°C or colder, the minimum temperature is approximately r min(met$temp, na.rm = TRUE)°C. This is more reasonable for the locations and period represented by the dataset.

The valid elevations range from r min(met$elev, na.rm = TRUE) to r max(met$elev, na.rm = TRUE) meters. This range is plausible for weather stations in the continental United States because some locations are below sea level while high-elevation stations may be located in mountainous areas.

## 6. Calculate summary statistics

The next step is to select the observations from the weather station at the maximum elevation.


```{r}
elev <- met[
  !is.na(met$elev) & met$elev == max(met$elev, na.rm = TRUE),
]

summary(elev)
```

### Correlations


```{r}
cor(elev$temp, elev$wind.sp, use = "complete.obs")
cor(elev$temp, elev$hour, use = "complete.obs")
cor(elev$wind.sp, elev$day, use = "complete.obs")
cor(elev$wind.sp, elev$hour, use = "complete.obs")
cor(elev$temp, elev$day, use = "complete.obs")
```

The correlation between temperature and wind speed indicates whether higher temperatures tend to occur with higher or lower wind speeds. The correlations involving hour and day help identify possible daily and monthly temporal patterns. These correlations should be interpreted cautiously because time variables are cyclical and the relationships may not be linear.

## 7. Exploratory graphs

### Distributions of the key variables

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

hist(
  met$elev,
  breaks = 100,
  main = "Distribution of Weather-Station Elevation",
  xlab = "Elevation (meters)",
  col = "steelblue",
  border = "white"
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

hist(
  met$temp,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Distribution of Temperature",
  xlab = "Temperature (°C)",
  col = "tomato",
  border = "white"
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

hist(
  met$wind.sp,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Distribution of Wind Speed",
  xlab = "Wind speed",
  col = "darkseagreen",
  border = "white"
)
```

The distributions of elevation and wind speed appear right-skewed. A log transformation may be useful in a later statistical analysis. However, special care would be required for zero or negative observations before applying a logarithmic transformation.

### Location of the highest-elevation station


```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

leaflet(elev) |>
  addProviderTiles("OpenStreetMap") |>
  addCircles(
    lat = ~lat,
    lng = ~lon,
    opacity = 1,
    fillOpacity = 1,
    radius = 100,
    popup = ~paste(
      "Elevation:", elev, "meters",
      "<br>Latitude:", lat,
      "<br>Longitude:", lon
    )
  )
```

The map displays the location of the weather station with the highest recorded elevation.

### Create a date-time variable

```{r}
elev$date <- with(
  elev,
  ymd_h(paste(year, month, day, hour), tz = "UTC")
)

summary(elev$date)

elev <- elev[order(elev$date), ]
head(elev)
```

### Temperature time series


```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

plot(
  elev$date,
  elev$temp,
  type = "l",
  main = "Temperature at the Highest-Elevation Weather Station",
  xlab = "Date and time",
  ylab = "Temperature (°C)",
  col = "firebrick",
  lwd = 1
)
```

### Wind-speed time series


```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

plot(
  elev$date,
  elev$wind.sp,
  type = "l",
  main = "Wind Speed at the Highest-Elevation Weather Station",
  xlab = "Date and time",
  ylab = "Wind speed",
  col = "navy",
  lwd = 1
)
```

### Summary of time-series patterns

The temperature time series shows variation over time, including a daily pattern in which temperatures generally rise during the day and fall during the evening or early morning. The plot may also contain short-term fluctuations caused by changing weather conditions.

Wind speed varies more irregularly over time. It contains periods of relatively low wind speed interrupted by larger peaks. Compared with temperature, wind speed does not appear to follow as smooth or consistent a daily cycle. Missing wind-speed readings may also produce gaps in the plotted line.

## 8. Questions about the data

After examining the dataset, I would ask a collaborator the following questions:

1. What exact value or code is used to indicate missing data for each variable?
2. Why were elevation values of 9999 entered instead of being recorded as missing?
3. What are the measurement units for wind speed?
4. Were all weather stations calibrated using the same procedures and equipment?
5. Are the recorded hours in local time or Coordinated Universal Time?
6. Were the temperature measurements taken at exactly the same time as the wind-speed measurements?
7. Why are there so many missing wind-speed observations?
8. Do multiple rows at the maximum elevation represent one station or several stations at the same elevation?
9. Were any quality-control procedures applied before the dataset was released?
10. Are the unusually low temperature observations measurement errors, coding errors, or valid readings?

## Conclusion

This exploratory analysis identified the weather station with the maximum valid elevation and examined its temperature and wind-speed measurements over time. Elevation values equal to 9999 were treated as missing, and implausibly low temperatures were removed according to the lab instructions. The highest-elevation station displayed temporal variation in both temperature and wind speed, with temperature showing a clearer daily pattern and wind speed showing more irregular fluctuations.
